Messages.Author: Lupus Australis
Messages.Body:
Imagine the following situation:

John has a Fragment of Nod in play, and a Monocle of Clarity. Mary has
the Barrens in play, and and only 2 cards left in her library. John needs
pool to survive, and has a Blood Doll and a Minion Tap in his hand.
Realistically, to survive, he will either need to play a Blood Doll by
this round at the latest, or the Minion Tap by next round at the latest.
Playing Minion Tap this round would be the best option, but he is afraid
that Mary will play a Sudden Reversal if he does so. So to help him
decide what to do, he asks "If I play Minion Tap this turn, will you play
Sudden Reversal?"

Mary looks at her hand, and sees no SRs. However, she knows that she has
one more SR left in her deck, and a 50% chance of being able to get it by
means of the Barrens. She decides that, since she doesn't know the
answer, she is entitled to guess, and says "Yes".

John then taps the Fragment and Draws two cards, one of which is a second
Minion Tap. John decides that playing the Minion Tap on his next round
will give him better odds than playing the Blood Doll on this one, and
decides to play the first Minion Tap to force the SR out of Mary's hand.

Mary taps the Barrens, but fails to draw the SR.

Mary does not play SR, rendering her answer inaccurate. She says that she
is off the hook because one only must abide by ones answer "if possible".

Question is: Was Mary within her rights to say "yes" to John's question
when she did not know that the answer would be accurate? Had she said
"no" she would have been able to guarantee her answer.

Let's now make the question a little different, and imagine that there are
100 cards left in Mary's library, and she knows only 1 is an SR. It is
from her POV still possible that she be able to play an SR, but very
unlikely. Assuming a "yes" answer is permissable in the first case, would
it be permissable in this one as well?

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
Lupus Australis <jbwh...@dorsai.org> wrote:
> John has [...] a Monocle of Clarity. [...] he asks "If I play Minion Tap

> this turn, will you play Sudden Reversal?"
>

> Mary looks at her hand, and sees no SRs. [but could draw one]

> She decides that, since she doesn't know the
> answer, she is entitled to guess, and says "Yes".

Badly worded. Since she has to answer and the question involves the
future and both "yes" and "no" repesent possible truths (to the best of her
knowledge), she can answer with either.

She will then be bound to abide by that answer "if possible".

> John then [...]

> decides to play the first Minion Tap to force the SR out of Mary's hand.
>
> Mary taps the Barrens, but fails to draw the SR.
>
> Mary does not play SR, rendering her answer inaccurate. She says that she
> is off the hook because one only must abide by ones answer "if possible".

She is correct, by clear card text.

> Question is: Was Mary within her rights to say "yes" to John's question
> when she did not know that the answer would be accurate? Had she said
> "no" she would have been able to guarantee her answer.

The answerer is not required to give answers that they can guarantee to
abide by. It they were, the "if possible" clause would not be present.

Mary's answer was valid, since it was true at the time (to the best of
Mary's knowledge, she could play SR by the time John plays his Minion Tap,
since she didn't know when that would be or what cards she would draw
before that time).

> Let's now make the question a little different, and imagine that there are
> 100 cards left in Mary's library, and she knows only 1 is an SR. It is
> from her POV still possible that she be able to play an SR, but very
> unlikely. Assuming a "yes" answer is permissable in the first case, would
> it be permissable in this one as well?

Yes, for the same reasons.

Perhaps John would be better off asking "do you have an SR in your hand
and, if so, will you play it if I play Minion Tap this turn?"

--

The question wasn't badly worded. Lupus' statement taht Mary is
"entitled to guess" is badly worded.

> difficult to word without leaving a loophole open. That's why most questions
> about the future tend to be about intent.

Which are actually questions about the present. Present intent.
Which are different from questions about the future.

>

Incorrect. It is one question. And, as you say, Mary is required to give one

answer "no".

turn, she must answer "yes".

Messages.Author: Christopher Chew
Messages.Body:
Please excuse me for not following the thread so flame away if this is
redundant.

The take I have always understood is that the answer you give 'must' be
followed and you would thereby be bound to that answer. In this case she could
not say for certain that she will play sudden reversal so thereby she must say
no committing her to that action (even if she were to draw the SR.)

It is incumbent upon the person with the monocle to ask those question that
can receive a yes or a no. Some examples:

Q:Will you attack me with harrod next turn?
A:No (this obligates you to not attacking the next turn with harrod)
Q:Will you bleed me next turn?
A:Yes (this obligates you to bleeding with someone next turn)
Q:Can you wake next turn if I tap you out?
A:No (then you may not wake even if a card come up that allows you to)

It was always easiest if we thought of the monocle predicting the future.

I am sure this will generate some criticism so blast away.

-Chris

Messages.Body:
On Wed, 2 Dec 1998, Christopher Chew wrote:

> Please excuse me for not following the thread so flame away if this is
> redundant.
>
> The take I have always understood is that the answer you give 'must' be
> followed and you would thereby be bound to that answer. In this case she could
> not say for certain that she will play sudden reversal so thereby she must say
> no committing her to that action (even if she were to draw the SR.)

I'm not sure you understand the consequences of your position.

> It is incumbent upon the person with the monocle to ask those question that
> can receive a yes or a no.

I would tend to agree, but this only works if you carry the position to
it's logical extreme, as I have tried to do.

> Some examples:
>
> Q:Will you attack me with harrod next turn?
> A:No (this obligates you to not attacking the next turn with harrod)

He would not be able to say "yes" by your standards, because of not being
able to guarantee that this would be possible. He cannot guarantee that
he will be ready, or that the necessary cards will still be in his hand.

If Harrod were a Brujah, you would not even be able to guarantee a "no"
answer because of the possibility of Brujah Frenzy.

> Q:Will you bleed me next turn?
> A:Yes (this obligates you to bleeding with someone next turn)

An outcome you cannot guarantee. The only possible answer would be "no"
by your standards, since you cannot guarantee that you will have ready
minions with at least 1 blood (not to mention the technicality of whether
you mean "bleed" or "attempt to bleed").

Thus, you could always make someone not bleed you by asking them if they
will.

> Q:Can you wake next turn if I tap you out?
> A:No (then you may not wake even if a card come up that allows you to)

Right. But while you can guarantee a "no" answer, can you guarantee a
"yes"? Suppose an effect causes you to discard a card at random, and you
lose that wake you were counting on. By your standards the respondent
must again always say "no" to this question.

> It was always easiest if we thought of the monocle predicting the future.

Well, that's the idea. It was never very good at predicting the future,
because we are talking about a real Jyhad game in which the future is in
fact unpredictable. It main infamy comes from its abuse to manipulate
events. That's the part i don't like.
